topics.title: Multi-Table Joins
topics.frequency_signal: Every Glassdoor SQL screen for the role mentions at least one multi-table join problem. (Sample fixture; real run cites real URLs.)

worked.prompt: Return each production with the total spend across all its payments. Sort by total spend descending. Business motivation: leadership needs a one-page overview of which productions are burning the most cash this fiscal month so we can prioritize close reviews.
worked.solution:
SELECT
  p.production_id,
  p.title,
  SUM(pmt.amount_usd) AS total_spend
FROM productions p
JOIN payments pmt USING (production_id)
GROUP BY p.production_id, p.title
ORDER BY total_spend DESC;
walk: Joining productions to payments on production_id is the right move because every payment must be tied to a production for spend to count.
Used INNER JOIN (just JOIN) here, not LEFT JOIN, because productions with zero payments would show as NULL totals and clutter a leadership view.
USING (production_id) is shorthand for ON p.production_id = pmt.production_id when the column has the same name in both tables.
SUM aggregates payment amounts per production after grouping; without GROUP BY this would error.
GROUP BY needs every non-aggregated SELECT column. We include p.production_id and p.title to satisfy that.
ORDER BY total_spend DESC puts the highest-burn productions on top, matching what leadership scans first.
If we wanted to include zero-payment productions, the query becomes a LEFT JOIN with COALESCE(SUM(amount_usd), 0).
worked.self_explain_prompt: Before moving on, explain in your own words why an INNER JOIN was the right default here and when you would switch to LEFT JOIN.

worked.prompt: For each production, return the top 3 vendors by total spend, with their rank. Tiebreak on vendor_id. Business motivation: vendor concentration risk reviews require a per-production view of who is taking the most money.
worked.solution:
WITH per_vendor AS (
  SELECT
    production_id,
    vendor_id,
    SUM(amount_usd) AS total_spend
  FROM payments
  GROUP BY production_id, vendor_id
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT
    production_id,
    vendor_id,
    total_spend,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY production_id
      ORDER BY total_spend DESC, vendor_id ASC
    ) AS rk
  FROM per_vendor
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rk <= 3;
walk: Two-step CTE: first sum per vendor per production, then rank. Doing both in one query is possible but harder to read.
ROW_NUMBER picked over RANK because we want exactly 3 rows per production even when totals tie. RANK would give 1, 1, 3 on a tie at the top.
PARTITION BY production_id resets the ranking inside each production.
ORDER BY total_spend DESC, vendor_id ASC: the second key is the tiebreak the prompt asked for.
Filtering with rk <= 3 in the outer SELECT, not in the window function itself, because window functions can't be in WHERE.
If the requirement was 'top 3 including ties' the answer would use DENSE_RANK and the row count per production could exceed 3.

worked.prompt: Return productions where, in any single fiscal month, a single vendor accounted for over 60% of that month's total spend on the production. Output the production, fiscal month, offending vendor, and their share. Business motivation: surface single-vendor concentration risk that current reports miss.
worked.solution:
WITH monthly_vendor AS (
  SELECT
    production_id,
    DATE_TRUNC('month', paid_on) AS fiscal_month,
    vendor_id,
    SUM(amount_usd) AS vendor_spend
  FROM payments
  GROUP BY production_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', paid_on), vendor_id
),
monthly_total AS (
  SELECT
    production_id,
    fiscal_month,
    SUM(vendor_spend) AS month_spend
  FROM monthly_vendor
  GROUP BY production_id, fiscal_month
)
SELECT
  mv.production_id,
  mv.fiscal_month,
  mv.vendor_id,
  ROUND(100.0 * mv.vendor_spend / mt.month_spend, 1) AS pct_share
FROM monthly_vendor mv
JOIN monthly_total mt USING (production_id, fiscal_month)
WHERE mv.vendor_spend > 0.60 * mt.month_spend;
walk: Two CTEs: spend per vendor per month, then total per month. Joining them gives the share.
DATE_TRUNC('month', paid_on) buckets payments by fiscal month. Postgres syntax. In Presto/Trino it would be date_trunc('month', paid_on).
Joining monthly_vendor to monthly_total on (production_id, fiscal_month) gives each vendor row the denominator it needs.
Filter with mv.vendor_spend > 0.60 * mt.month_spend. Stating it as a multiplication avoids a divide-and-compare which can lose precision on integer types.
ROUND to one decimal place for human-readable output; the comparison itself uses the unrounded values to avoid false negatives at the boundary.
If thresholds vary by production tier, you'd join in productions with a CASE on tier; documented as the obvious next iteration.

faded.prompt: Return each production with the total spend across all its payments. Sort by total spend descending.
faded.scaffold:
SELECT
  p.production_id,
  p.title,
  _____(pmt.amount_usd) AS total_spend
FROM productions p
_____ JOIN payments pmt USING (_____)
GROUP BY p.production_id, p.title
ORDER BY total_spend _____;
faded.solution:
SELECT
  p.production_id,
  p.title,
  SUM(pmt.amount_usd) AS total_spend
FROM productions p
INNER JOIN payments pmt USING (production_id)
GROUP BY p.production_id, p.title
ORDER BY total_spend DESC;
walk: First blank is the aggregator. SUM, not COUNT, because we want dollars not row counts.
Second blank is the join type. INNER (or just JOIN) drops productions with no payments.
Third blank is the join column.
Fourth blank is the sort direction. DESC because leadership scans top-down.

       ROUND(100.0 * mv.vendor_spend / mt.month_spend, 1) AS pct_share
FROM monthly_vendor mv
JOIN monthly_total mt USING (_____, _____)
WHERE mv.vendor_spend _____ 0.60 * mt.month_spend;
faded.solution:
WITH monthly_vendor AS (
  SELECT production_id,
         DATE_TRUNC('month', paid_on) AS fiscal_month,
         vendor_id,
         SUM(amount_usd) AS vendor_spend
  FROM payments
  GROUP BY production_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', paid_on), vendor_id
),
monthly_total AS (
  SELECT production_id, fiscal_month, SUM(vendor_spend) AS month_spend
  FROM monthly_vendor
  GROUP BY production_id, fiscal_month
)
SELECT mv.production_id, mv.fiscal_month, mv.vendor_id,
       ROUND(100.0 * mv.vendor_spend / mt.month_spend, 1) AS pct_share
FROM monthly_vendor mv
JOIN monthly_total mt USING (production_id, fiscal_month)
WHERE mv.vendor_spend > 0.60 * mt.month_spend;
walk: Date function blank: DATE_TRUNC, used twice consistently inside the same CTE.
Join columns blank: (production_id, fiscal_month) is the composite key tying vendor spend to its month total.
Comparator blank: > stages the threshold check as a multiplication so we avoid integer-divide precision loss.

retrieval.prompt: Return the count of distinct vendors who received at least one payment in 2026.
retrieval.selfExplain: Why use a half-open interval [2026-01-01, 2027-01-01) instead of BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31'?
retrieval.explanation: Half-open intervals are correct for date-and-timestamp comparisons regardless of whether the column is a DATE or a TIMESTAMP. BETWEEN with the year-end date silently misses any timestamps between 2026-12-31 00:00:01 and 23:59:59. The COUNT DISTINCT collapses rows so a vendor paid twice in 2026 still counts once.

retrieval.prompt: Return productions whose total spend in April 2026 increased by more than 50% over their March 2026 total. Output production, March total, April total, growth rate.
retrieval.solution:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT production_id,
         DATE_TRUNC('month', paid_on) AS month,
         SUM(amount_usd) AS month_spend
  FROM payments
  WHERE paid_on >= '2026-03-01' AND paid_on < '2026-05-01'
  GROUP BY production_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', paid_on)
),
pivoted AS (
  SELECT production_id,
         SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-03-01' THEN month_spend END) AS march_total,
         SUM(CASE WHEN month = '2026-04-01' THEN month_spend END) AS april_total
  FROM monthly
  GROUP BY production_id
)
SELECT production_id, march_total, april_total,
       ROUND(100.0 * (april_total - march_total) / march_total, 1) AS growth_pct
FROM pivoted
WHERE march_total IS NOT NULL
  AND april_total > 1.5 * march_total;
retrieval.selfExplain: Why pivot with conditional aggregation instead of using LAG over months?
retrieval.explanation: Either approach works. Conditional aggregation reads more naturally when the comparison is between two specific months and you want both totals as columns. LAG is preferred when the comparison generalizes to N months or you need a rolling pattern. The march_total IS NOT NULL guard prevents division-by-zero false positives for productions that started in April.

retrieval.prompt: Identify pairs of productions whose payment date ranges overlap and that share at least one vendor. For each overlapping pair, return the productions, the shared vendors, and the overlap window.
retrieval.solution:
WITH shared_vendors AS (
  SELECT a.production_id AS prod_a,
         b.production_id AS prod_b,
         a.vendor_id
  FROM (SELECT DISTINCT production_id, vendor_id FROM payments) a
  JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT production_id, vendor_id FROM payments) b
    ON a.vendor_id = b.vendor_id
   AND a.production_id < b.production_id
)
SELECT sv.prod_a,
       sv.prod_b,
       string_agg(DISTINCT sv.vendor_id, ',') AS shared_vendors,
       GREATEST(pa.start_date, pb.start_date) AS overlap_start,
       LEAST(pa.end_date, pb.end_date) AS overlap_end
FROM shared_vendors sv
JOIN productions pa ON pa.production_id = sv.prod_a
JOIN productions pb ON pb.production_id = sv.prod_b
WHERE GREATEST(pa.start_date, pb.start_date) < LEAST(pa.end_date, pb.end_date)
GROUP BY sv.prod_a, sv.prod_b, pa.start_date, pa.end_date, pb.start_date, pb.end_date;
retrieval.selfExplain: Why the a.production_id < b.production_id constraint in shared_vendors?
retrieval.explanation: Self-joining a table on a shared attribute (vendor) without an ordering constraint produces every pair twice (P101,P102) and (P102,P101) plus self-pairs (P101,P101). The strict-less-than constraint gives unordered pairs and excludes self. The Allen's-intervals overlap test is GREATEST(starts) < LEAST(ends); if true, the windows overlap. string_agg coalesces multiple shared vendors into one cell.
